title: The two thrones, the empty hall and the burning water
subtitle: In which the great give one another gifts while elsewhere chairs tip over and ships hold their breath.
lede: What happened yesterday is told onward today.

threads.title: The Iran war and the bottleneck
threads.summary: Hormuz, Houthis, oil, diplomacy in New York.

threads.title: The two thrones
threads.summary: Trump and Xi, trade, AI, Taiwan.

threads.title: The eastern field
threads.summary: Ukraine, winter, G20, books as a target.

figures.name: Donald Trump
figures.text: Receives the rival as a guest; his own press only after a court order. Promises friendship, delivers an extension.

figures.name: Xi Jinping
figures.text: Accepts the eagle, speaks of stability, draws circles around Taiwan and wants AI under human control — in the circle of those who build it.

figures.role: The speaker in the thinning hall
figures.name: Benjamin Netanyahu
figures.text: Speaks to a house that in part stands up and leaves. Calls it cowardice. The pictures do their work.

figures.name: Masoud Pezeshkian
figures.text: Denies the bomb, offers seven days, demands an American decision. War and negotiation in one sentence.

figures.name: Leo XIV
figures.text: Comes into a secular, quarrelling France and walks the same carpet as reasons of state.

figures.role: The absent man at the table
figures.name: Vladimir Putin
figures.text: Invited to Miami, condemned in Brussels, present in Ukraine by fire — including on paper and binding.

yesterday.title: The eagle lands, the hall waits.
yesterday.teaser: Xi arrives in Washington. UN week reaches its loudest day.

body:
There are mornings when the world behaves as if someone had slid two books into each other: one with gilt edges, one with soot on the margins. 25 September 2026 is such a morning. In Washington the carpet is still being brushed. In New York chairs stand crooked because their occupants have left the hall. And on the Red Sea someone is counting missiles, not metaphors.

I. The feast of the two thrones

Donald Trump has walked Xi Jinping across the White House lawn like a host who wants to show that the estate still holds. A new helicopter pad. Military pomp. In the evening a state banquet whose front row is not only ministers but the keepers of the new oracles: Bezos, Musk, Huang, Altman, Cook. 1 2

The gift of the evening is an eagle of metal. America hands China its heraldic bird across the table. Xi speaks of “strategic stability” and warns of the old trap in which rising and established powers tear each other apart because they cannot do otherwise. Taiwan, he lets it be known, is to be handled with care. Artificial intelligence, the two men agree, should remain subject to the human — a sentence that, in a room full of tech princes, lands about as well as a vow of temperance at a wine feast. 3 4

What was actually decided remains thin. A trade truce extended by two months. Much ceremony, little treaty. Friendship is proclaimed loudly so that no one notices how quietly the clauses speak.

While Xi is welcome in the house, three previously barred American newsrooms — among them CNN and Politico — are allowed back onto the grounds after a judge’s ruling. So on the same day the White House receives a head of state whose media landscape is among the least free in the world, and is forced to let its own press back in. The irony needs no narrator. It takes a seat by itself. 5

II. The hall that empties

A few hundred kilometres farther east, in the building that once promised nations would talk to one another instead of shooting, Benjamin Netanyahu steps to the General Assembly podium. Before the first sentence has settled, delegations leave. Chairs fold. The hall thins. Netanyahu calls those who go “moral cowards”. 6 7

Outside in New York demonstrators are arrested, including faces from the film business. Inside, the Israeli prime minister defends the war, praises Trump as a partner and rejects the charge of genocide. It is a speech for his own camp and against the room in which it is given. Those who stay hear an indictment. Those who leave turn the indictment into choreography. 8

At the same hour Iran’s president, Masoud Pezeshkian, says Tehran wants no nuclear weapon; the supreme leader has declared the pursuit of one unholy. At the same time he speaks of an America that must decide whether the war should end — and of a seven-day plan that could reopen the Strait of Hormuz and revive nuclear talks. Whether that is diplomacy or the art of buying time while diesel in Europe marks record prices will be shown in the next chapter. 9 10

III. The burning water

In the Red Sea and over Saudi Arabia the language is shorter. The Houthis fire ballistic missiles; Riyadh speaks of six intercepted rounds on Yanbu, Taif, military targets. France announces soldiers and radar to protect a Saudi energy hub. Oil still flows, but dearer, more awkward, more nervous. The Strait of Hormuz remains the bottleneck at which industrial society notices that it drinks from a hose. 11 12

Anyone who wishes can read this as a sideshow. Anyone honest sees the bill: every projectile over the Red Sea is also a sentence at the European pump, in the Ukrainian winter and on the table of the two thrones.

IV. The field in the east and the books

Over Ukraine drones and missiles come down again. The authorities count the dead — farm workers in the east, people in Kyiv. Russia, correspondents report, strikes not only positions but warehouses full of books. A publisher whose stock has burned twice speaks the sentence of the day, which needs no poetry: Moscow holds books more dangerous than military kit. 13 14

In Copenhagen the Danish military intelligence service warns: an open invasion of NATO states is unlikely, hybrid attacks more likely. In Miami, where the G20 is soon to meet, Washington has invited Putin. Brussels wants the invasion condemned there — whether or not the invitee appears. Zelenskyy, meanwhile, speaks of a decision by Trump to give Ukraine a Patriot licence. The war is in its fifth year far enough along that even invitations to banquets act like weapons. 15

V. The white guest in an uneasy country

In Paris Pope Leo XIV begins a four-day journey. Red carpet at the Élysée, a handshake with Emmanuel Macron, later Notre-Dame, UNESCO, a prayer with the young. A pope who after Africa now visits the old heartland of the Church, while France argues over assisted dying and abuse and Macron sends soldiers to the Red Sea. Spirituality and reasons of state share the same calendar. 16 17

VI. What the book must not omit

At the margins, and therefore easy to skip, two people die in a house fire in Lucca. Pakistan and Afghanistan keep firing on the border. In Morocco a party wins an election. Off Mexico’s Pacific coast Hurricane Polo churns the water. In the Philippines President Marcos confirms the pardon of Mary Jane Veloso, who spent years on death row in Indonesia. Great politics loves the stage. Life itself is distributed among the footnotes. 18

And over it all, invisible as weather, the yield on long American bonds rises to levels last known in another neighbourhood of capitalism. Money has no morals, but it has a memory for risk. 19

The chronicler’s finding

If this story had a moral, it would be cheap. It has none. It has figures who give one another eagles while elsewhere books burn. It has a hall that empties and a sea that does not. It has a pope on the red carpet and farm workers who do not get up again.

The World Book does not close today. It only leaves a finger between the pages and waits for 26 September. Tomorrow we will see whether the two months of trade peace hold, whether Hormuz remains a gate or becomes a weapon, and whether the hall of nations fills once more — or whether empty chairs have by now become part of the furniture.
